name: Deepa Krishnan
presenting_complaint: Fever, palpitations and agitation on a background of Graves disease

medications: Carbimazole 20 mg daily (self-reports missing doses for the past 2 weeks)
medical_history.social: Works as a teacher. Non-smoker. Minimal alcohol. Recently unwell with a chest infection.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 41-year-old woman with known Graves disease presents febrile (39.4 C), agitated and confused with a rapid irregular pulse. She admits to missing her carbimazole for two weeks and has had a recent respiratory infection. She is flushed, tremulous and diaphoretic with an irregularly irregular tachycardia of 148 and signs of early heart failure. This is thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky high). Obs: BP 150/70, HR 148 (AF), RR 26, SpO2 96%, Temp 39.4 C, GCS 14.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Confirm thyrotoxic history: known Graves disease, current antithyroid therapy and ADHERENCE (carbimazole missed for 2 weeks)
Identify the PRECIPITANT: recent infection/URTI, surgery, iodine/contrast load, trauma, thyroxine overdose, non-adherence, DKA, labour
Storm symptom screen: fever, palpitations, agitation/confusion, tremor, heat intolerance, diarrhoea/vomiting, weight loss
Cardiac symptoms: palpitations, chest pain, dyspnoea, symptoms of heart failure
Counsel/document agranulocytosis warning for thionamides: present urgently if sore throat or fever; document allergies and medications
objective: Apply a storm severity score (Burch-Wartofsky) documenting fever, tachyarrhythmia, CNS and GI features
12-lead ECG (confirm AF/tachyarrhythmia), continuous cardiac monitoring, assess for heart failure (JVP, crackles, oedema)
Bloods: TFTs (free T4/T3, TSH), TSH-receptor antibodies, FBC (baseline WCC before thionamide), UEC, LFTs, calcium, BGL, blood cultures/septic screen, troponin
Examination: goitre/bruit, eye signs, temperature, hydration, conscious level; thyroid imaging if indicated
Regular temperature and neuro obs; look for a source of sepsis (CXR, urine, cultures)
assessment: Thyroid storm (decompensated thyrotoxicosis) precipitated by carbimazole non-adherence plus intercurrent infection — a medical emergency with significant mortality
New/decompensated atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and early high-output heart failure
Exclude and treat concurrent sepsis as precipitant; consider DKA and other precipitants
Recognise time-critical treatment sequence: beta-blocker, then thionamide, then iodine (at least 1 hour AFTER thionamide), then corticosteroid, plus supportive care
plan: Beta-blocker FIRST for adrenergic control: propranolol 60-80 mg PO 4-hourly (or 0.5-1 mg IV slowly, titrated) to control heart rate; use cautiously with cardiac monitoring given heart failure (consider short-acting IV esmolol in a monitored setting)
Thionamide to block hormone synthesis: propylthiouracil 200 mg PO/NGT 4-hourly (preferred in storm as it also blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion), OR carbimazole 20 mg 4-6-hourly
Iodine (Lugol's iodine or potassium iodide) to block hormone release — give at least 1 HOUR AFTER the thionamide, never before
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV 6-hourly (reduces T4-to-T3 conversion and treats relative adrenal insufficiency)
Treat the PRECIPITANT: empirical antibiotics for the respiratory infection/sepsis after cultures; do not overlook the trigger
Supportive care: IV fluids, active cooling and paracetamol for fever (AVOID aspirin — displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins), treat AF/heart failure, VTE prophylaxis
Urgent referral to ICU and endocrinology; high-dependency monitoring
Serial obs, ECG and repeat FBC/LFTs; monitor for thionamide agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity

critical_errors: Giving iodine before (or without) the thionamide — providing substrate feeds the thyroid and worsens the storm; iodine must follow the thionamide by at least 1 hour
Failing to identify and treat the precipitant (missed carbimazole plus intercurrent infection/sepsis)
Using aspirin for fever (displaces thyroid hormone and worsens thyrotoxicosis) instead of paracetamol and cooling
must_not_miss: Correct treatment sequence: beta-blocker, then thionamide, then iodine (>=1 hour later), then corticosteroid
Precipitant identified and treated (non-adherence and infection)
Thyroid storm recognised as an emergency with ICU/endocrine escalation
Hydrocortisone given to block peripheral conversion
